name: Ramayana
info: The Ramayana is a Sanskrit epic of ancient India, traditionally attributed to Valmiki, which tells the life and journey of Rama, prince of Ayodhya, and has shaped Hindu life and the arts of South and Southeast Asia.

facts.made: Traditionally attributed to the sage Valmiki; scholars see it as a growth of centuries from an oral source, with the first and last books generally held to be later additions
facts.form: A Sanskrit epic poem of about 24,000 shlokas (couplet verses) in seven kandas and about 500 sargas (chapters)
facts.where: Read in northern and southern recensions and many manuscripts; a critical edition was compiled at Maharaja Sayajirao University of Baroda in the 1960s and 1970s
facts.known: Rama's fourteen-year exile; the abduction of Sita by Ravana; Hanuman's leap to Lanka; the war with Ravana; Rama rajya as the ideal of just rule; Diwali and Ramlila

t: Hindus count the Ramayana, with the Mahabharata, among the Itihasas; it tells of Rama, held to be the seventh avatar of Vishnu, and portrays ideal sons, brothers, wives and kings.
Scholars place its oral composition roughly in the 8th to 4th centuries BCE, with later stages reaching the 3rd century CE; books two to six are the oldest.
It was retold in nearly every Indian language and in Buddhist and Jain versions, and became the Reamker of Cambodia, the Ramakien of Thailand and the Kakawin Ramayana of Java.
dyk: In the Jain versions of the epic it is Lakshmana, not Rama, who kills Ravana, and Jain texts hold that Ravana will become a future Tirthankara.
ev: Robert P. Goldman's probable date for the oral composition of Valmiki's Ramayana
Later stages of the text extend to about this time; a panel at Nagarjunakonda shows Bharata meeting Rama
The Kakawin Ramayana is written in Central Java
Kamban writes the Ramavataram in Tamil
Tulsidas composes the Ramcharitmanas in Awadhi
Akbar commissions an illustrated simplified text for his mother, Hamida Banu Begum
The Oriental Institute at Baroda compiles a critical edition from dozens of manuscripts
Robert P. Goldman completes an English translation of the critical edition

sections.origins:
The Ramayana, also known as the Valmiki Ramayana, is a Sanskrit epic of ancient India traditionally attributed to the sage Valmiki. Its name joins Rama and ayana, "journey", and so means "Rama's journey". It belongs to the Itihasa, narratives of past events that include teachings on the goals of human life; modern scholars often place it in the genre of epics.

Scholarly estimates for its primary oral stage range from the 8th–5th to the 5th–4th century BCE, "although the legends constituting it go back farther in time", and later stages extend to the 3rd century CE. Robert P. Goldman gives 750 to 500 BCE as the probable date of its oral composition, noting that the narrative does not mention Buddhism, does not reflect the later prominence of Magadha, and names Ayodhya rather than Saketa or Shravasti as the capital of Kosala. Goldman and Sally Sutherland Goldman later placed it around the middle of the first millennium BCE.

In the epic's own frame story, Valmiki asks the sage Narada whether a righteous man is left in the world and is told of Rama; after seeing two birds shot, Valmiki creates the shloka metre and composes the poem, which he teaches to Rama's sons Lava and Kusha.
sections.content:
Rama, son of King Dasaratha of Ayodhya and his first wife Kausalya, wins Sita, daughter of King Janaka of Mithila, by stringing and breaking a bow no one else could string. On the eve of his crowning, his stepmother Kaikeyi claims two boons and has him exiled to the forest for fourteen years so that her son Bharata may succeed. Rama accepts; Sita and his brother Lakshmana go with him, and Bharata rules only on Rama's behalf.

In the forest Ravana, king of Lanka, carries Sita away with the help of a demon disguised as a golden deer. Rama allies with the Vanaras of Kishkindha, and Hanuman, the greatest of his devotees, leaps across the sea, finds Sita in the Ashoka grove and sets fire to Ravana's citadel. A bridge is built, and in the war that follows Rama kills Ravana and installs his brother Vibhishana as king. Sita proves her fidelity by entering a fire from which the god Agni restores her, and Rama returns to Ayodhya to be crowned; his reign, Rama rajya, is described as just and fair. The last book tells of Sita's exile, the birth of Lava and Kusha and Rama's last days.

The epic depicts the duties of relationships through ideal characters and joins philosophical and ethical teaching to its story.
sections.making:
In its extant form the poem has over 24,000 couplet verses called shlokas in seven kandas: Bala, Ayodhya, Aranya, Kishkindha, Sundara, Yuddha and Uttara. It is regarded as one of the longest epic poems ever written. Romesh Chunder Dutt wrote that it is "a growth of centuries, but the main story is more distinctly the creation of one mind."

Books two to six are the oldest part. Differences of style and contradictions in the narrative have led scholars including Hermann Jacobi to regard the first and last books, the Bala Kanda and the Uttara Kanda, as later additions, and both are absent from the oldest manuscript. Some hold that the Uttara Kanda contradicts the rest of the epic's picture of Rama and dharma; M. R. Parameswaran argues that its treatment of women and Shudras, in the stories of Sita's abandonment and the killing of the ascetic Shambuka, shows it to be a later insertion.

The text was handed down orally along two regional paths for a long time before being fixed in writing, producing a northern and a southern recension with profound verbal differences. The northern tradition moved toward a simpler gloss, while the more conservative southern one forms the backbone of modern critical editions.
sections.reception:
The Ramayana strongly influenced later Sanskrit poetry and Hindu life and culture, and its figures became central to the cultural consciousness of many Hindu and Buddhist nations. Its chief moral lesson was the importance of virtue, in the life of a citizen and in the ideal of the state as Rama rajya. Around thirty-three commentaries were written on it; the tilaka, bhushana and shiromani are the best known.

Tamil literature refers to the story from the Sangam age, in the Akananuru and Purananuru, and in the Silappatikaram, Manimekalai and the Alvar poets, before Kamban wrote the Ramavataram in the 12th century. Regional retellings followed in Telugu, Assamese (Madhava Kandali's Saptakanda Ramayana), Bengali (Krittibas Ojha), Odia, Kannada, Malayalam, Marathi and Gujarati, and Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas of 1576 recast it in Awadhi in the spirit of bhakti. The Mughal emperor Akbar commissioned an illustrated simplified text around 1594 and dedicated it to his mother.

Buddhists told it as the Dasaratha Jataka, in which Rama is a previous birth of the Buddha and there is no Ravana, and Jains as Vimalsuri's Paumachariyam and later works, in which Rama renounces his kingdom and becomes a monk.
sections.survival:
As with many oral epics, many versions survive, and the story told in north India differs in important respects from that kept in the south and in Southeast Asia. A 6th-century manuscript from West Bengal presents the epic without the Bala and Uttara Kandas. Oral and folk versions continue: the Gond Ramayani of the Gondi people, with Lakshmana as its hero, and the Adiya Ramayana of Wayanad, in which Rama is tried in a tribal court for abandoning his pregnant wife.

In Southeast Asia the story became Cambodia's Reamker, whose manuscript is first mentioned in a 7th-century inscription and whose surviving text dates from the 16th century, and the Trai Bhet; the Kakawin Ramayana of Java, based on Bhatti's poem on the killing of Ravana rather than on Valmiki; the Balinese Ramakavaca, the Malay Hikayat Seri Rama, the Burmese Yama Zatdaw and the Thai Ramakien. The Maranao Maharadia Lawana of the Philippines was first written down when Juan R. Francisco and Nagasura Madale documented and translated it in 1968.

A critical edition was compiled in the 1960s and 1970s by the Oriental Institute at Maharaja Sayajirao University of Baroda from dozens of manuscripts, and Robert P. Goldman completed its English translation in 2016.
sections.legacy:
The Ramayana has had a profound impact on art and culture across the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia, with the exception of Vietnam. Its scenes appear in terracottas, stone sculptures, bronzes and paintings, from the 3rd-century panel at Nagarjunakonda to the 9th-century reliefs of Prambanan in Java and the murals of Wat Phra Kaew in Bangkok. In Java and Bali it is a source of moral guidance and of wayang shadow puppetry, the Balinese kecak dance and the Ramayana Ballet staged before Prambanan.

Hindus connect Diwali, the festival of lights, with Rama's return to Ayodhya, and dramatic enactments called Ramlila take place across India and the Indian diaspora. Rampur is the commonest name for villages and towns in much of India, and "Ram Ram" is used as a greeting.

Modern retellings include versions by C. Rajagopalachari and R. K. Narayan and novels by Ashok Banker and Amish Tripathi. Gopal Sharman's play The Ramayana has had more than 3,000 performances, and films from Lanka Dahan in 1917 to Ramanand Sagar's television series of 1987 have carried the story to new audiences.

summary: The Ramayana, a Sanskrit epic traditionally attributed to Valmiki and composed orally over centuries from about the mid-first millennium BCE, tells of Rama's exile, the abduction of Sita and the war with Ravana. Retold in Buddhist, Jain and many regional versions across South and Southeast Asia, it shapes festivals, art and ideas of just rule.
